units.title: 1. Chronic Inflammatory Demyelinating Disorders of the CNS
units.guide:
The chapter opens by listing the chronic inflammatory demyelinating disorders of the CNS: multiple sclerosis, neuromyelitis optica, anti-MOG antibody disease, sarcoidosis and chronic graft-vs-host disease, with a note that non-inflammatory demyelination means osmotic demyelination from rapid sodium correction.
MS is defined as chronic inflammatory demyelination of the subcortical area, brainstem, spinal cord and cortical area while sparing the peripheral nerve system and organ systems.
Features are autoimmune disease, females greater than males, significant family history and HLA DR2/15; risk factors are EBV, smoking, vitamin D deficiency and high socio-economic status.

units.title: 2. Pathogenesis, Target Antigens, Imaging Correlates and the BBB Figure
units.guide:
Pathogenesis is inflammation, demyelination, gliosis and secondary neuronal injury; astrocytes disrupt the blood-brain barrier and raised VEGF causes exudation from capillaries, giving hyperintense lesions on T2 and contrast enhancement on T1.
T cells and B cells act on the target antigens myelin basic protein and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein, producing demyelination with loss of saltatory conduction and cumulative axonal destruction that branches into cortical atrophy and progressive neuronal damage.
The blood-brain-barrier figure labels tight junction, pericyte, astrocyte, endothelial cell, microglia, basement membrane, peg-socket junction, leukocyte and neuron.

units.title: 3. Disease Patterns, Sensory and Motor Features and Optic Neuritis
units.guide:
Disability curves divide MS into relapsing-remitting in 90%, secondary progressive in 5-6% following the relapsing-remitting form, and primary progressive, for which the printed Rx is anti-CD20 with ocrelizumab.
Major features are long-tract sensory manifestations, the m/c complaint, with tingling, numbness, paraesthesia, hypaesthesia, unpleasant sensations and allodynia; UMN motor weakness with loss of strength and speed, loss of tone, loss of dexterity, spasticity and exercise-induced fatigue; and optic neuritis that is unilateral, asymmetric if bilateral, with retrobulbar pain, anterior-pathway involvement, drug responsiveness and diplopia.

units.title: 4. Minor Features, Other Presentations and the McDonald Criteria
units.guide:
Minor features are ataxia, vertigo, bladder involvement, Lhermitte sign, dementia and myokymia, while other presentations include bilateral internuclear ophthalmoplegia, bilateral trigeminal neuralgia, pseudobulbar involvement and acquired pendular nystagmus.
McDonald criteria need dissemination in time plus dissemination in space: dissemination in time is satisfied clinically or radiologically by two lesions four weeks apart, a new T2 hyperintense lesion, or a T1 lesion enhancing with contrast; dissemination in space requires two lesions at different sites among juxtacortical, periventricular, spinal cord and infratentorial (cerebellar and middle cerebellar peduncle).

units.title: 5. Ancillary Symptoms, MRI Patterns, CSF and VER
units.guide:
Ancillary symptoms are Uhthoff's phenomenon with unilateral blurring of vision during a hot shower, Lhermitte's symptom from neck flexion which is also seen in compressive myelopathy, and the Pulfrich phenomenon in which a two-dimensional image is perceived as three-dimensional.
T2 hyperintensities are common in periventricular white matter and typical in the corpus callosum as Dawson's fingers, illustrated by the MRI panels showing hyper-intense lesions and a periventricular lesion; CSF shows oligoclonal bands with IgG increased in 90%, and the visually evoked response has a sensitivity of 80-85%.

units.title: 6. Acute Attack Therapy and Disease-Modifying Options
units.guide:
Acute attacks and relapse-remission episodes are treated with IV steroids, and the prevention list is grouped by route.
Infusables are natalizumab (anti-α4 integrin, side effect progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy), ocrelizumab for the primary-progressive type and alemtuzumab (anti-CD52); injectables are glatiramer acetate and IFN β.
Orals are fingolimod as a sphingosine receptor modulator, teriflunomide as a dihydroorotate dehydrogenase inhibitor and dimethyl fumarate.

units.title: 7. NMO (Devic's Disease) and Its Distinction from MS
units.guide:
Neuromyelitis optica, also called Devic's disease, is a chronic inflammatory demyelinating disease of females more than males, around 40 years of age, associated with autoimmune disease such as SLE in 40% of cases, and driven by antibody against aquaporin 4.
Clinically optic neuritis is present and myelitis is variable, with hearing loss also listed: optic neuritis is bilateral and symmetrical with chiasmal involvement, poor response to treatment and severe visual loss, while myelitis shows long-segment involvement with longitudinal extension of transverse myelitis, poor prognosis and a monophasic course; recurrent intractable hiccup is attributed to area postrema involvement.
Investigations show oligoclonal bands in only 30% and a normal MRI brain, and treatment is steroids with plasma exchange.

units.title: 8. Anti-MOG Antibody Disease and Acute Disseminated Encephalomyelitis
units.guide:
Anti-myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein disease is printed as covering optic neuritis, myelitis, aquaporin-4-negative NMO spectrum disorders and acute disseminated encephalomyelitis.
ADEM is a disease of children under 12 years with males more than females, usually post-infectious after measles more often than chicken pox with an incubation of 4-21 days, or post-vaccination, and pathologically driven by molecular mimicry of myelin basic protein and myelin oligodendrocyte protein.
Clinically it combines acute inflammatory demyelination of white matter predominantly with grey matter, basal ganglia and thalamus in a monophasic course with large foci of hyperintensity and fluffy lesions, together with encephalitis producing seizure, raised intracranial tension, loss of consciousness, bilateral hypertonia with hyper-extensive response, meningismus and a wide motor and sensory repertoire.

units.title: 9. ADEM Imaging and the Printed ADEM versus MS Comparison
units.sec: ADEM Imaging and the ADEM-MS Table
units.guide:
Investigation of ADEM is MRI showing large foci of hyperintense lesions, illustrated by sagittal brain and cervical cord and axial FLAIR images captioned hyper-intensity in MRI.
The comparison table separates ADEM (under 12 years, males more than females in children, triggers and constitutional symptoms present, bilateral optic neuritis, complete myelopathy rare, encephalopathy common, monophasic, large usually symmetrical lesions, centripetal location, mass effect and grey matter involvement) from MS (over 12 years, females more than males at 3:1, no triggers or constitutional symptoms, unilateral optic neuritis, complete myelopathy common, encephalopathy less common, relapsing-remitting, variable-size asymmetric lesions, periventricular location and none of the other features).
